w: Eccentric English poet Edward James spent three decades and his fortune building over 30 concrete follies through a subtropical waterfall gorge: spiral stairs that end in midair, doorways framing nothing, a house that will in fact have five or six floors, all half-swallowed by jungle.
s: Surrealist concrete ruins swallowed by jungle
why: One of the world's great surrealist gardens, built alone by an eccentric heir deep in the Sierra Gorda rainforest

w: Duke Vicino Orsini carved a woodland of giant volcanic-stone monsters in the 1550s: a screaming ogre mouth big enough to picnic inside, a leaning house, an elephant crushing a soldier. Meant to unsettle rather than delight, it predates every later fashion for landscaped gardens.
s: 16th-century garden of giant stone monsters
why: Considered the oldest sculpture garden of the modern era, built to disturb rather than please

w: Niki de Saint Phalle spent two decades raising 22 mirror- and mosaic-clad giants, one for each major arcana card. Visitors climb inside a voluptuous Empress sheathed in glass tile -- the artist's home during construction -- and wander among towers, sphinxes and a maze of reflective monsters.
s: Walk-in mosaic giants, one per tarot card
why: A monumental outsider-art garden you physically climb inside

w: A reclusive paper-mill worker spent fifty years alone carving nearly 500 concrete figures in his parents' garden: yoga-posed athletes, soldiers, animals, self-portraits, many fitted with real human teeth. He never explained the work and died in 2010; the park remains exactly as he left it.
s: 500 self-taught concrete figures in a pine forest
why: An entire outsider-art garden built alone by one obsessive rural sculptor over half a century

w: Painter Jacques Majorelle spent forty years building a studio garden of bamboo groves, cactus beds and lily channels around a cobalt-blue villa, a shade now trademarked as Majorelle Blue. Abandoned after his death, it was rescued from demolition in 1980 by Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Berge.
s: Cobalt-blue villa garden of cacti and bamboo
why: One of the most photographed gardens on earth, saved from the bulldozer by a fashion designer

w: Founded in 1983 at the foot of Wutong Mountain, seventeen specialty gardens hold over 8,000 plant species, including some of Asia's largest cycad and palm collections, threaded around a lake and the historic Hongfa Buddhist temple.
s: 8,000-species garden below Wutong Mountain
why: One of China's largest botanical collections, still largely bypassed by foreign visitors

w: Planted from 2005 on hills stripped bare by the catastrophic 2003 firestorm, 94 separate forests hold rare and endangered trees from around the world, alongside a bonsai collection and a giant bronze-and-stone sculpture called the Wide Brown Land overlooking Lake Burley Griffin.
s: 94 forests of rare trees on fire-scarred hills
why: A young arboretum that turned bushfire devastation into one of the world's largest living tree collections

w: A retired physician and a sculptor turned their working dairy farm into 30 acres of garden rooms filled with kinetic scrap-metal creatures, a repurposed grain silo, ponds and allees, opened to the public as a nonprofit only in 2016 after decades as a private passion project.
s: Kinetic scrap-metal sculptures on an old dairy farm
why: Quietly one of New England's most inventive gardens, still little known outside regional circles

w: Built directly on the roof of a circular expressway loop junction, a spiral ramp climbs past 1,000 trees, cherry blossoms, pine and a bamboo grove to a ring-shaped park suspended above the traffic it was built to muffle. Below, the interchange itself keeps moving cars in tight circles.
s: A ring-shaped garden atop a highway interchange
why: One of the strangest garden sites anywhere -- an entire park balanced on a highway loop

w: Privately funded and built on leftover land wedged between converging motorways, eight separate garden islands are stitched together by footbridges and tunnels, holding more than 120,000 trees and shrubs -- a forest reclaimed from a highway interchange in one of the world's fastest-growing cities.
s: Eight garden islands stitched over a motorway junction
why: A forest that reclaimed leftover motorway land instead of a park site

w: Artist Cesar Manrique carved a terraced amphitheater out of a disused quarry and lava tube, planting thousands of cacti from five continents around a restored 19th-century windmill. A giant articulated metal cactus sculpture, visible for miles, marks the entrance off the coastal road.
s: A cactus garden carved into a collapsed lava tube
why: Landscape art fusing raw volcanic terrain with a serious desert-plant collection

w: Some 45 million flowers, replanted seasonally, are trained over archways, vintage cars and a life-size Airbus A380 replica in what is billed as the world's largest natural flower garden. It survives the desert heat on drip irrigation fed by treated wastewater, closing each summer when temperatures peak.
s: 45 million flowers shaped into planes and castles
why: An absurdist flower spectacle grown entirely inside the Dubai desert

w: Wrapped around a bend of the Luosuo River since 1959, this is the largest outdoor tropical plant collection on earth: over 13,000 species across 38 themed zones, including giant Victoria water lilies that open at dusk and a clock flower that blooms on an almost hourly schedule.
s: 13,000 tropical species around a river bend
why: The world's most complete outdoor tropical botanical collection, still off most itineraries

w: Entrepreneur Alan Gibbs commissioned massive abstract works from two dozen renowned sculptors -- a multi-storey paper clip, a bridge built from stacked cubes, a life-size steel giraffe -- and scattered them across 1,000 grazed acres overlooking the harbour. Free, but open only a handful of days a year by booking.
s: Giant abstract sculptures grazed by farm animals
why: One of the world's largest private sculpture parks, rarely open and little known beyond New Zealand

w: Eighteen fully enclosed garden rooms recreate 4,000 years of garden history with no fences or plant labels breaking the illusion -- a Maori kitchen garden, an Italian Renaissance courtyard, a Ming Chinese scholar's garden, and a deliberately playful Surrealist Garden of oversized furniture.
s: Garden rooms spanning 4,000 years of design
why: A theatrical garden-of-gardens approach almost no other institution attempts

w: Founded in 1929 on the eastern edge of the capital, Central Asia's oldest botanical garden acclimatizes subtropical and Mediterranean species against a harsh, arid continental climate -- a rare stretch of unregimented green space inside one of the world's most closed and least-visited capitals.
s: Central Asia's oldest garden, in a closed capital
why: A century-old botanical institution inside one of the world's least-visited capital cities

w: A cast-iron and glass complex begun in 1874 within the grounds of the royal palace, its 57-metre domed Winter Garden houses camellias, orange trees and plant collections gathered from the former Belgian colonies. Still part of a working royal residence, it opens to the public only a few weeks each spring.
s: A domed glass palace open three weeks a year
why: A genuine palace of glass the public can only see for a few weeks each spring

w: Elsie Reford began transforming her salmon-fishing camp into a garden in 1926, eventually raising the northernmost great garden in eastern North America, famous for its blue Himalayan poppies. Since 2000 it has also hosted an annual International Garden Festival of experimental installations.
s: The northernmost great garden in eastern North America
why: A subarctic-latitude heritage garden plus an annual avant-garde design festival

w: Opened in 2018 on reclaimed wetland, its glasshouse recreates the plant zones of twelve world cities under one roof. A dedicated seed library lets visitors borrow packets of seeds like books, expected to grow them at home and voluntarily return saved seed from the harvest.
s: A seed library where you borrow seeds like books
why: A lending library built entirely around seeds instead of books

w: A privately run garden descends a steep river gorge just north of Ubud's crowded center, threading an orchid house, medicinal-plant trail, bamboo forest and lily ponds along the ravine walls, with hanging bridges giving views down to the water below.
s: A terraced garden down a jungle river gorge
why: A quieter, less commercialized alternative to Bali's famous rice terraces, minutes from Ubud

w: Established in 1966 in a forested tribal district, Gujarat's largest botanical garden lays out separate plots recreating the state's arid, moist-deciduous, bamboo and scrub-forest habitats side by side, along with cactus, orchid and medicinal-plant collections along seven kilometres of paths.
s: A biodiversity park recreating Gujarat's forest types
why: An obscure state garden preserving forest habitats most visitors to India never encounter

w: Sixty hectares of sub-Andean forest above Ibague hold major orchid, bromeliad and palm collections and double as an active research station -- several new Anthurium and Xanthosoma species have been formally described here and published in international botanical journals.
s: A forest garden that keeps discovering new plants
why: An active taxonomic research garden still finding species new to science

w: Opened in 2022 inside a protected stone-pine reserve above where the Atlantic meets the Mediterranean, ten thematic zones make use of natural springs and a mild oceanic microclimate to grow a broader plant palette than Tangier's dry surrounding hills would otherwise support.
s: A brand-new garden in a pine reserve above the Atlantic
why: Tangier's first dedicated botanical garden, barely a few years old

w: At the foot of the Hex River Mountains, greenhouses and outdoor beds hold nearly 3,000 succulent species from around the world, set against roughly 400 species that grow wild in the surrounding Karoo semi-desert -- one of the planet's richest concentrations of succulent diversity.
s: Nearly 3,000 succulent species at the Karoo's edge
why: Arguably the single best place on Earth to see succulent plant diversity in one visit

w: Five hundred acres built almost entirely for tourism turn out to be scientifically serious: a dedicated Cycad Gene Bank holds more than 280 species, alongside orchid nurseries, a stone garden of imported boulders and avenues of elaborately clipped topiary shaped into animals and pagodas.
s: 500 acres and one of the world's largest cycad banks
why: An outsized private tourist garden with a genuinely important cycad conservation collection

w: Carmelite monks began planting exotic trees here in 1628 behind walls meant to keep the outside world out. A 1643 papal bull threatened excommunication for anyone who damaged a tree; Mexican cypress, Australian bunya pines and Californian redwoods now shade a fairy-tale neo-Manueline palace hotel.
s: A walled 17th-century forest guarded by papal decree
why: One of Europe's oldest protected arboretums, historically enforced by threat of excommunication

w: Built without a single nail, timber halls and a golden pavilion floating on a lotus pond recreate Tang-dynasty garden design in miniature beside the Chi Lin Nunnery. Rockeries, a bonsai collection and a wooden bridge complete the illusion, wedged into a dense public-housing district of Kowloon.
s: A Tang-dynasty garden built without a single nail
why: An exacting recreation of 1,000-year-old garden design dropped into a dense modern district

w: Intha farmers weave long strips of water hyacinth and lake-bottom mud into buoyant beds anchored with bamboo poles, then pole between the rows by canoe to tend tomatoes and flowers. Some floating plots have been worked by the same families for generations, forming entire farming villages that ride the water.
s: Tomato farms rooted to woven mats that float
why: An entire agricultural landscape that literally floats on the surface of the lake
